subject: mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?

messages.author: 82889e926eb5165e
messages.subject: mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?
parts:
Hi all

I have being working with some models where the posterior distributions are not normally distributed, so I have used the highest density point (HDP) as the point estimate and best central tendency measure to describe the posterior distribution.

I have being using this function to find the highest density point

my_mode <- function(x){ ## where x is the vector of save iterations of a parameter in stan
  dx <- density(x)
  return(mode=dx$x[which.max(dx$y)])
}

When the posterior distribution is clearly not normally distributed (so the mean is not the best point estimate to describe it), is this method to estimate the highest density point appropiate? or the HDP should be calculated in another way?

Thanks

--- Mauricio Garnier-Villarreal

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?
parts:
If the marginal distribution is not Gaussian, then using the density() function which defaults to a Gaussian kernel seems a bit suspect.

The marginal modes do not seem that important to me. If you want the multivariate mode, it would be something like

best <- which.max(sapply(get_logposterior(posterior), FUN = tail, n = nrow(posterior)))
posterior_mode <- as.matrix(posterior)[best,]

Ben

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?
parts:
>
> Hi, Ben. Mayhap a bit off-topic, but if the bandwidth is small enough, why should the kernel being Gaussian be problematic? On a small enough scale, it probably doesn't make that much of a difference.

He’s trying to get a mode, so the kernels have to be tuned ever so carefully that the KDE isn’t multimodal.

But as has been ranted on the list before, the MAP is not particularly informative, particularly in complex models. There is no one value that summarizes a distribution, and if you use one try to at least use one that is a proper expectation (like the mean or the median or, even better, a credible interval).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?
parts:
I know there is no one way to summarize a disrtibution. I always include the credible intevals. But only the credible intervals is not enough, I want to use an expectation. I am having cases of unimodal skew posteriors, in these cases we know the mean is not a proper expectation, so I was looking for the highest desnsity point as the most likely estimate in the posterior. If the distribution is actually normal the highest density point and the mean would be the same, but when they are different it seems to me that the highest density point is a better expectation than a bias mean.

Why would it be prefer a mean or median instead of the highest density point in a skew unimodal distribution? Or is there a better way to describe it that I am not seeing?

Thanks

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?
parts:
Expectations are means by definition.

There's an extensive literature on estimators that'll
tell you everything you need to know about point estimates
in terms of bias and variance (for instance, dividing
by (n-1) in a sample variance calculation gives you the
unbiased estimate, whereas dividing by n gives you the
maximum likelihood estimate).

Posterior means minimize expected square error, posterior medians
minimize expected absolute error, whereas posterior modes aren't
optimizing anything other than posterior density. People use
all of them in various settings where it's too expensive to
calculate with the full posterior or where they want a single
summary statistic.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?

> Expectations are means by definition.
>
> There's an extensive literature on estimators that'll
> tell you everything you need to know about point estimates
> in terms of bias and variance (for instance, dividing
> by (n-1) in a sample variance calculation gives you the
> unbiased estimate, whereas dividing by n gives you the
> maximum likelihood estimate).
>
> Posterior means minimize expected square error, posterior medians
> minimize expected absolute error, whereas posterior modes aren't
> optimizing anything other than posterior density. People use
> all of them in various settings where it's too expensive to
> calculate with the full posterior or where they want a single
> summary statistic.

There are simple cases (like the exponential family in some parameterizations)
where the maximum density aligns with a proper expectations (usually the
mean) but this is not robust to the choice of distribution! Use a percentile
if you’re worried about people misinterpreting the mean.

messages.author: 20758fda448fdbda
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] mean vs mode (highest density point) of the posterior distributions?
parts:
I can forsee some times where looking at the "most probable" or "most common" value may be of use. For example, if a parameter in general can be in one of two neighborhoods, I'd like to know which of the two neighborhoods it is more likely to be in. Concretely, the parameter either hovers around 1 (about 40% of the time) and 20 (about 60% of the time). Having a mode of 20 is more informative to me than a mean of 12.4. Of course, the distributional shape is of most importance in that case, but the mode lets me know that 20 is more likely than 1.

Avi
